blocks.text: In the Hebrew form of Esther, God’s name, direct speech, miracles, covenant, Torah, temple, and explicit prayer are absent. Readers may see the timing of the king’s sleepless night and Mordecai’s unexpected honor as hidden providence, but the narration itself does not explicitly say that God caused each action or approves every tactic in the story.

This chapter stands at the center of Esther’s pattern of dramatic reversal: Haman arrives intending Mordecai’s death, imagines royal honor for himself, and must instead publicly honor Mordecai. The larger story carries this reversal forward, as Haman is later exposed at Esther’s second banquet and killed on the structure he prepared for Mordecai. Readers differ over how to classify Esther’s blend of Persian court color, stylized symmetry, satire, and improbability; labels such as history, court tale, comedy, or historical novella each emphasize different features rather than settling every historical question.

sections.title: A Reversal That Shapes the Story
